doc.title: Rick Montalbano interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 12, 2011

title: Ricky sits in: Foster Brooks, Dominick Bruno and the wedding band
summary: At about seven Ricky played a blues on stage at the Hotel Oneida for Foster Brooks, and Dominick Bruno wanted to form a band around him. He later played in his father's eighties wedding band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: That’s great. Do you remember the first time you took him out on a gig?

He would sit in a lot. And one time when he was about seven I was playing at the time for Dominick Bruno. Do you remember the name Dominick Bruno? He owned a club in Syracuse called Three Rivers Inn for years and years. It was the big showroom of Central New York, all the acts of Sammy Davis Jr. and Bobby Darin and all those people. Everyone played there. That was the place. And he owned the place. The place burned down at one point. It was fortunate because he happened to get the piano and the organ out of there just the night before it burned down, amazingly.
What kind of — so now he owned the Hotel Oneida and we were doing shows in the Hotel Oneida. Did you work any for me there?

Because I used to get all my friends on the gigs, you know J.R. [Monterose] played them and it was hilarious times. And Foster Brooks was the act. You remember Foster Brooks with his drunk act and all that. So it was on a Sunday and I went with Jill and Ricky. I took them along to the gig. And we were there a little early and the crowd was already there and Dominick decided let’s go on now, but the band hadn’t showed up yet. So I had to play Foster Brooks on. So I just said “Ricky, come up and play, we’ll just play a blues, come up on the stage.” He didn’t think anything of it. He just went up to I think maybe Jimmy Johns’ drums at the time, and just sat down behind the drums and we played a blues [scats] and he played and Foster Brooks came out and he starts doing his act and he turned back and again it was like one of those moments. He looked back and here’s this little thing behind the drums. I mean nobody announced it or made a big deal in any way of it. Actually no one knew, we just went out and played him on. So he was quite taken with that. And the funniest part was Dominick Bruno, when he saw it, he just flipped and he decided we were going to put a group together with, do you remember the Harmonicats? With the little harmonica? What was the name Jerry? Anyway he was a friend of Dominick’s. That was one of the groups that used to play at Three Rivers. So Dominick was going to put this band together with Ricky and me and this guy and a couple of other guys and we were going to go out on the road and he was just out of his mind over this idea of a little kid and a little guy playing together somehow. So yeah, so that’s what would happen. He would come and he would sit in on gigs. And then when I © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -19-

had a wedding band in the eighties I mean he could come up and play the whole gig with us and sometimes he would. And you would never notice, there was never — okay we’re playing with a kid who doesn’t know, we’ve got to make concessions. It was never that. He just played the gig. So he got a lot of experience early on.
